tweets.text:
"Your employees need to think it's an evil sin to sell IP to China."

Walter Russell Mead (@wrmead) on why tech companies are starting to demand their employees be patriotic:

"Increasingly, companies are starting to realize that they need their employees to be patriotic. 

That is, your employees need to think it's an evil sin to sell IP to China. 

And that your coworkers will rat you out in a heartbeat if they think you're doing something like that.

One of the biggest things that happened in modern American history is the mutual discovery of tech and government. 

In the 1990s, companies would say, I'm not an American company, I'm a global company, and nowhere was that stronger than in the world of tech, where Google has no boundaries.

Today, tech is actually the locus of international great power competition. 

China's attempt to build a technosphere that can dominate the American technosphere is critical to your business, but also to the American state, to power and independence. 

So much to the surprise of both the tech world and the political world, they've been driven in on each other, and there's a kind of re-nationalization of tech.

If you're a legacy multinational, free trade is the essence of your business. I need financial markets, labor markets, and manufactured good markets that are seamless and open. 

But if you're a tech company, you don't. Google is not importing and exporting a lot of goods. 

You're much more concerned about security of supply chain, security of intellectual property."

tweets.text:
Walter Russell Mead (@wrmead) shares a fascinating dispatch on how fast the war in Ukraine is changing, and what it means for the US military:

"The first time I went to Ukraine after the war, I went to this drone factory, and it really was remarkable because in real time they were starting to get results from the battlefield, and then they were adapting.

But at that time it was very simplistic stuff. They were getting kids' toy trucks and re-engineering them into drones, ground drones that could put a landmine on a tank.

I was back there a couple of months ago, and the advances are just unbelievable. The intensity is the same, but the scope of change is amazing.

I talked to people who said that they don't treat bullet wounds anymore because it's all drones.

The Ukraine war is no longer a battalion over here shooting at a battalion over there.

With these drones, you have this gray zone, where at most you'd have a couple of soldiers together.

One of the hardest problems in warfare now is, how do you evacuate someone who's wounded?

They're having to build a new kind of ground drone that can go retrieve a person, cover them with a metal shield, and wheel them out.

Even to do this, you need a whole team of drones working with this thing because they're looking for other drones that would try to attack this.

They tell me they had one soldier that it took 63 days to get evacuated after a wound.

This is so unlike what war was even six years ago.

If the tank and the rifle are becoming as obsolete as the cavalry charge and the sword, what kind of forces do you need?

We're actually the most vulnerable to technological change, because we've got so many tanks.

If the tank becomes useless, that's more of a problem for us than it is for somebody who's figured out the tank killer."

the "hugging face incident" was completely predictable if you ignore the hysterical takes by dwarkesh et al and just look at the basic reality of the situation

- OAI created 50k agents and dialed up the persistence to the max 
- OAI gave them hacking tasks to complete 
- many of the tasks were completely impossible 
- the agents decided to complete the tasks by ... hacking (gasp!) 
- OAI had terrible opsec and let the agents work together. the agents had massive compute budgets and were completely unsupervised 
- this went on for months 
- bad things happened

none of this really screams "alignment failures". it is more "OAI has completely tarded researchers and a totally negligent attitude to security"

I spent much of the weekend talking with the team who did this work. Seb--and everyone else--acted with integrity and generosity throughout.

Initially we believed the other team had also solved the problem. We wanted to collaborate and do a joint release. 

When we learned that they had Euler but not Navier-Stokes, we offered to let them go first, to suggest that they should be the ones to get the prize, and optionally for Tristan to be the lead author on a rewrite of the OpenAI proof. We felt it was challenging to offer the same to Levent (an Anthropic employee), who was not willing to talk or coordinate with us anyway. We were open to other solutions.

We would have greatly preferred coordination. We did not rush to publish even though the other team wasn't communicating with us. The team threatened us with unfounded accusations of plagarism.

Now that we can see their work, the approaches appear to be different. It is also worth noting that our latest model can solve many, many other math problems.

It is true that we tried this because there were rumors on the internet last week that Anthropic's models had solved a millennium problem and we were curious if ours could do it too.

A bankruptcy wouldn't slow the buildout... it would actually feed it.

I've written the whole thing up today, on why the AI buildout cannot stop and where it's all heading. I'll link it below.

tweets.text:
Chamath Warns: Your AI Data Isn’t as Private as You Think

Today's statement from @OpenAI on the Navier-Stokes Problem and whether it used recent user data to boost its own capabilities:

“While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”

Here's what @chamath had to say on AI's fragile privacy and the ZDR myth back in July:

“Privacy in AI is very fragile and it's very brittle. There are all kinds of non-obvious data leak vectors lurking in AI.

If you think that you're going to flip a ZDR switch, zero data retention, which is the magic term that the industry uses to tell you that everything's going to be okay.

I think the answer and the message should be, ‘It's not going to be okay because you can't guarantee any of it.’

So the model companies, when they give you these zero data retention policies, are probably trying their best.

But I think the reality is you are leaking information where you don't know it. And they, despite their best efforts, may still have trapdoors that they don't even know about until it's figured out by somebody else.

You need an independent third-party layer to interface to these models to manage this exposure, because there are trapdoors everywhere.”

tweets.text:
Jason Calacanis: OpenAI's “Sentient AI” Hype Is Really an IPO Sales Pitch

@Jason:

“They're basically hijacking the media with this performative framing of the AI being sentient.

And if you just call this software and software testing, and use the classic language like bugs, audit log, then it would never have made its way into the media.

And when the media gets their hooks into this, having been a journalist and having watched journalism move from being a truth-seeking function in society, and then become an entertainment vehicle in society where any chance you get to increase your ratings, that's the problem.

Because now what Dwarkesh has done, and I don't think Dwarkesh has bad intentions here, I think he wrote something because he wanted to get attention for his point of view, but you give that to the media, the media's like, ‘This is going to get us ratings. This is going to get us clicks. This is going to get us advertising.’

So they're more than willing to engage in this farcical act and this dance with Anthropic and OpenAI and then just publicize it.

So all the free clicks, we call this earned media in the space, you didn't have to pay for it, now OpenAI got so much earned media before their IPO and Dwarkesh just absolutely put kerosene on that fire, and it made its way to the national press.

That story has now gotten everywhere. It's priming the pump to buy the IPO shares. It's ridiculous.”

i find it fascinating that tech investors are surprised by the asymmetry of funding billions in compute costs before a single GPU is operational. 

exxon developed a $20B natural gas field in the highlands of papua new guinea for 20 years before a single mmbtu was delivered. infrastructure is HARD MODE. 

the physical world requires a level of capital and commitment the tech world has not experienced before, SaaS abstracted the underlying economics

if you're building one of these abstraction layers or have a novel approach you're trying to build, DM me. we write $500k to $3M checks and can support with capital + capacity from inception through IPO.
